setup.zh: 傍晚，山门外：舅舅在等你，镖师葛六也在。「进了门，头一件事，有人找你收钱。给不给，你自己掂量。」
setup.en: Dusk outside the gate: your uncle is waiting, and so is the escort Ge Liu. "Once you're through the gate, first thing, someone comes to collect money. Pay or don't — weigh it yourself."

recap.zh: 开山门那天傍晚：舅舅在山门外等你，没让马三把你劝退；葛六说破了林子里那颗石子，又说「有人的地方，就有公中」。夜里，舅舅在泗水边的柳树底下埋了石蛋。
recap.en: The evening the gate opened: your uncle waited outside and would not let Ma San talk you out of it; Ge Liu named the pebble in the woods aloud, and said, "Wherever there are people, there's a common fund." That night your uncle buried Shidan under a willow by the Si.

en: Outside the gate, your uncle looks up.
"Wherever there are people, there's a common fund."

story.zh:
那天傍晚，新入门的弟子许出山门，跟送考的家里人说一句话，一炷香为限。执事把那面兵器架子抬上来了，小满取回了爷爷那张弓——第三排左数第七个，一个手指头也没人碰过——背在背上，跑出山门。

山门外的石坪边上，坐着葛六，短刀横在膝盖上，腰里的钱袋瘪着。他看见小满，招了招手，道：「杂灵根，进了？」小满道：「进了。」葛六道：「林子里那颗石子，是马三一锭银子买的。我没接，他扣了我五两。我说了，也没用。」他站起身，把短刀插回腰里，「进了门，头一件事，有人找你收钱——一个月三块灵石，先得交出去一块。有人的地方，就有公中。给不给，你自己掂量；你这样的，掂量得清。」说完，他顺着石阶下山去了。小满站在那里，把这两句话在心里各记了一笔。

石坪那头，有人叫他：「满子。」是老周，阿禾她爹，裤腿上全是泥，在山门外头站了一整天，脸都晒脱了皮。他搓着手，想问又不敢问，憋了半天，道：「我家禾……」小满道：「进了。真灵根，中上。」老周愣了一愣，蹲下去，拿两只手捂着脸，捂了好一会儿，才站起来，从怀里摸出一个鸡蛋，塞给小满：「拿着。」山门里闪出阿禾来，一把拿了回去：「爹，他还欠我三个半。」转身进了山门。

舅舅站在第三百级石阶边上，青布长衫的下摆全是泥。他一看见小满，先不问考上没考上，从怀里摸出一个炊饼塞进他手里，这才问：「……考上了？」小满道：「外门。」舅舅一把抓住了他的胳膊，抓得死紧，这才看见他袖子上的血，脸一下子白了：「伤着哪儿了？」小满道：「不是我的。」

他把林子里的事说了。说得很短，说到「太华多远」，便说不下去了。舅舅听完，半天没出声，末了问：「他爹呢？」小满道：「拿了银子，天没亮就往北走了。」舅舅道：「……我来。」

马三从人堆里挤了过来，没理小满，把舅舅拉到一边，压低了嗓子，脸上堆着笑：「沈家舅舅，商量个事。杂灵根，下下之资，在山上熬也是白熬。你让他自己退了，今年的山风钱，免一年。」舅舅这一辈子，见了马三从来不抬头。这一回，他抬起了头：「不退。家里有孩子进了仙门的，马家不敢收租——这话，满县城都知道。」马三的笑一下子没了。他盯着舅舅看了好一会儿，道：「好。沈家的租，马家不收了。」他转过身，冲着家丁，嗓门放得大大的：「可后山是马家的山，山上的风也姓马。牵马，连夜回蒙山告诉老爷：从明儿起，沈老大进山，打一只兔子，交一只兔子。」又冲山门里头扬了扬下巴，「小宝，在山上给我看着他。」说罢，带着家丁下山去了。

舅舅望着他的背影，腰杆挺了一挺，又道：「当年，我也爬到了一百七十级——」小满道：「舅舅。」舅舅道：「……一百六十级。」

小满道：「舅舅，一百六十级那里，崖壁上刻满了字，都是在那一级上坐下过的人刻的。」舅舅不说话了。他把脸转过去，朝着泗水那边，看了很久。小满道：「舅舅，我替你走上来了。」舅舅没有回头。过了好一会儿，他才开口，声音有点哑，道：「……风大。」他拿袖子在脸上抹了一把，又抹了一把，然后转回来，把小满背上那张弓扶正了，把他的衣领翻好——翻衣领的那一下，同他姐姐一模一样——道：「回去吧。一炷香到了。」

小满走进山门，回头看，舅舅还站在那儿。石阶边上，牛棚里那个兖州来的孩子蜷着，脸朝着崖壁，他爹坐在旁边，一锅一锅地抽旱烟；廊下那个光脚的孩子蹲在山门边，考牌攥在手里，脚底板磨得渗着血丝。山门合上以后，舅舅挪过去，在他们中间坐下了。他没提自己的外甥，只道：「我当年，也没上去。下了山，去县里学打算盘，如今在济世堂做账房，娶了媳妇，生了个闺女。」他顿了一顿，又道：「挺好的。」兖州那个爹问他：「老哥，你当年，到底爬到了多少级？」舅舅想了一想，道：「一百六十级。」那是他这辈子，头一回，没有多说十级。

天擦黑，舅舅起身，在光脚的孩子跟前蹲下，道：「家在哪？」「汶上。二亩坡地，押给里正换的路费。说好了，考上了，五两银子赎回来。」舅舅把包袱里最后一块干粮塞给他，道：「会数数么？」「会。数到一千。」「济世堂缺一个抓药跑腿的，我去跟掌柜说。管吃管住，一个月三百文，地，一年赎得回来。」那孩子攥着那块干粮，看了他半天，道：「……你是谁？」舅舅站起身来，拍了拍膝盖上的土，道：「一个爬到一百六十级的。今夜先帮我挖个坑。」

他们没有往县城走。舅舅去林子口，跟守林的执事讨了石蛋。执事巴不得有人讨，连名册都没再翻。两个人一前一后，抬着一扇卸下来的牛棚门板，下了石阶，在泗水边一棵柳树底下，挖到半夜。舅舅是拿算盘的手，挖不深；光脚的孩子是种地的手，挖得深。埋好了，舅舅找了一块石头立在前头，不会刻字，拿炭在上头写了两个字：石蛋。光脚的孩子问：「他家里人知道么？」舅舅道：「不知道。」又道：「我记着。济世堂往北走货，我托人往沂水打听。」

走回山脚，马家包下的那家客栈门口，灯笼底下跪着一个人，是葛六：镖局的掌柜正把红绸从他的刀鞘上一圈一圈解下来，两个家丁把他的短刀折成了两截。葛六自己站起来，捡起那半截刀，往北边黑地里去了。舅舅没有停步。他把那孩子往身后拉了拉，转过身，朝着蒙山的方向，走进了夜里。
story.en:
Toward evening that day the new disciples were allowed out of the gate to say a word to the family who'd brought them, for the length of one stick of incense. The stewards had carried the weapons rack up; Xiaoman took his grandfather's bow back — third row, seventh from the left, not a finger laid on it — slung it on his back, and ran out of the gate.

At the edge of the terrace outside the gate sat Ge Liu, his short knife across his knees, his purse flat at his waist. He saw Xiaoman and beckoned. "Mixed root. In?" Xiaoman said, "In." Ge Liu said: "That pebble in the forest — Ma San bought it with a silver ingot. I didn't take it, so he docked me five taels. I said it out loud, and it did no good." He stood and slid the knife back into his belt. "Once you're through the gate, first thing, someone comes to collect money — three spirit stones a month, and one has to go straight back out. Wherever there are people, there's a common fund. Whether you pay is yours to weigh; someone like you can weigh it clear." And he went off down the stair. Xiaoman stood there and set each of those sentences down in his head.

Across the terrace someone called him: "Manzi." It was Old Zhou, Ah He's father, mud all up his trouser legs; he had stood outside the gate all day and his face was peeling from the sun. He rubbed his hands, wanting to ask and not daring, and at last managed: "My Ah He…" Xiaoman said, "In. True root, above the middle." Old Zhou stood stunned, squatted down, covered his face with both hands a long while, then stood, took an egg from his coat and pushed it at Xiaoman: "Take this." Ah He darted out of the gate and snatched it back: "Dad, he still owes me three and a half." And she turned and went back in.

His uncle stood by the three-hundredth step, the hem of his blue cotton gown all mud. The moment he saw Xiaoman, before asking whether he'd got in, he took a griddle cake from his coat and pushed it into his hand, and only then asked: "…Did you get in?" Xiaoman said, "Outer court." His uncle seized his arm and gripped it hard — and only then saw the blood on his sleeve, and went white. "Where are you hurt?" Xiaoman said, "It isn't mine."

He told what had happened in the forest. He told it short, and when he got to "how far to Taihua" he couldn't go on. His uncle heard him out and said nothing for a long time; at last he asked, "His father?" Xiaoman said, "Took the silver and went north before it was light." His uncle said, "…I'll see to it."

Ma San pushed out of the crowd, ignored Xiaoman, drew the uncle aside, and said low, all smiles: "Brother Shen, a word. A mixed root, lowest of the low — it's wasted effort sticking it out up here. Have him withdraw of his own accord, and this year's mountain-wind money is waived." All his life the uncle had never looked up at Ma San. This time he looked up. "He won't withdraw. A family with a child inside the immortal gate — the Mas daren't take rent from it; the whole county knows that." Ma San's smile vanished. He stared at the uncle a good while. "Fine. The Mas won't take the Shens' rent." He turned to his servants and raised his voice: "But the back mountain is the Mas' mountain, and the wind on it's surnamed Ma too. Saddle a horse, ride back to Mount Meng tonight, tell the master: from tomorrow, when old Shen goes up the mountain, one rabbit shot, one rabbit handed over." He jerked his chin toward the gate. "Xiaobao — keep an eye on him up here." And off he went down the mountain with his servants.

His uncle watched his back and straightened a little, and said again: "Back then, I climbed to step one hundred and seventy myself —" Xiaoman said, "Uncle." His uncle said: "…One hundred and sixty."

Xiaoman said, "Uncle, at step one hundred and sixty the cliff wall is covered in writing — all carved by people who sat down on that step." His uncle fell silent. He turned his face toward the Si and looked a long time. Xiaoman said, "Uncle, I walked up for you." His uncle didn't turn round. After a good while he spoke, his voice a little hoarse: "…Windy." He wiped his face with his sleeve, and wiped it again; then turned back, set the bow straight on Xiaoman's back, turned his collar straight — that turn of the collar exactly like his sister's — and said: "Go on back. The incense is out."

Xiaoman walked through the gate and looked back; his uncle was still standing there. By the stair the boy from Yanzhou who had shared the cowshed lay curled, face to the cliff, his father beside him smoking a long pipe, bowl after bowl; the barefoot boy from the veranda squatted by the gate, the tag in his hand, his soles worn raw and seeping blood. When the gate had closed, the uncle went over and sat down between them. He didn't mention his nephew; he said only: "I didn't get up either, back then. Came down, went to the county to learn the abacus; now I keep the books at the Jishi Hall, took a wife, had a daughter." He paused. "It's all right." The Yanzhou father asked him: "Old brother, how many steps did you really climb, back then?" The uncle thought a moment. "One hundred and sixty." It was the first time in his life he hadn't added ten.

As dusk came on, his uncle got up and squatted down in front of the barefoot boy. "Where's home?" "Wenshang. Two mu of hillside, pledged to the village head for the road money. The deal was, if I got in, five taels would buy it back." His uncle pushed the last piece of dry food from his bundle into the boy's hand. "Can you count?" "Yes. To a thousand." "The Jishi Hall needs a boy to fetch and run with the medicines; I'll speak to the owner. Board and lodging, three hundred coppers a month — you'll have the land back in a year." The boy held the food and stared at him a long time. "…Who are you?" His uncle stood and brushed the dirt off his knees. "Someone who climbed to the hundred-and-sixtieth step. Tonight, first, help me dig a hole."

They didn't take the road to the county town. His uncle went to the forest's edge and asked the keeping steward for Shidan. The steward was only too glad someone asked, and didn't even look at the register again. The two of them, one in front and one behind, carried a door taken off the cowshed down the stair, and under a willow by the Si they dug till midnight. His uncle had abacus hands and couldn't dig deep; the barefoot boy had farmer's hands and could. When it was done, his uncle found a stone and set it up at the head; he couldn't carve, so he wrote two words on it in charcoal: Shidan. The barefoot boy asked, "Does his family know?" His uncle said, "No." And then: "I'll remember. When the Jishi Hall ships goods north, I'll have someone ask around in Yishui."

Walking back to the foot of the mountain, they passed the inn the Mas had taken: under the lantern at its door knelt a man — Ge Liu. The caravan master was unwinding the red silk from his scabbard turn by turn, and two servants snapped his short knife in two. Ge Liu got up by himself, picked up the half knife, and went off north into the dark. His uncle didn't stop. He drew the boy behind him, turned, and walked off toward Mount Meng, into the night.

exits.means: pays the one stone to the common fund, keeps the peace for now

refuse.en: You have no spirit stones on you.

what.zh: 外门的「公中」：收了你一块灵石。
what.en: The outer court's "common fund": took one of your spirit stones.

story.zh:
小满把葛六那两句话，在心里掂量了一路。他掂量出来的是：一块灵石，买一个「懂事」，买马小宝一个月不来找麻烦。这笔账，眼下划得来。

第二天一早，饭堂门口，他从怀里摸出一块灵石，交了。马小宝掂了一掂，冲他笑，笑得跟他爹一模一样。

他心里却记了一笔：公中，一块。马小宝。
story.en:
Xiaoman weighed Ge Liu's two sentences all the way up the stair. What he weighed out was: one spirit stone buys "knowing his place", buys a month of Ma Xiaobao leaving him alone. For now, the sum comes out in his favour.

Next morning at the refectory door he took a spirit stone from his jacket and handed it over. Ma Xiaobao weighed it in his palm and grinned at him, a grin exactly like his father's.

But in his heart he entered a line: Common fund, one stone. Ma Xiaobao.

exits.means: refuses to pay the common fund

story.zh:
小满把葛六那两句话，在心里掂量了一路，掂量出来一个字：不。他把怀里的灵石一块一块放进他娘给的那个空钱袋里，叮，叮，叮。空钱袋里，头一回有了东西。

他知道往后会怎样：马小宝不会当着人的面动手，他会等。他爹就是这么收租的——先笑，再等，等你以为没事了，门就飞了。那就等。
story.en:
Xiaoman weighed Ge Liu's two sentences all the way up the stair, and weighed out one word: no. He put the spirit stones from his jacket one by one into the empty purse his mother had given him — *ting, ting, ting*. For the first time, the empty purse held something.

He knew what would come of it: Ma Xiaobao wouldn't lift a hand in front of people; he'd wait. That was how his father collected rent — grin first, then wait, wait till you think it's over, and then the door flies. Then let him wait.
